title: Bound the read, don't predict it
impact: Moonshot: ships the read routing exp 265 measured and then rejected, by replacing its admission test with enforcement. Exp 265 decided which `select()` calls could run on the calling isolate from the per-SQL row-count high-water mark exps 260/264 keep, and rejected itself because rows-returned bounds neither how large a row is (`SELECT * FROM photos WHERE id = ?` has a permanent high-water mark of 1 and one row can be a 5 MB image, copied unchecked because with no hop exp 236's blob wrap is suppressed), nor how much work precedes the first row, nor how long a chain of non-yielding reads holds the event loop. All three are closed here by checking the query against what it is producing rather than against its history: a 64-row cap, a 64 KB TEXT/BLOB payload cap read from the cell length *before* the copy, and a 10,000-VDBE-opcode cap enforced by a SQLite progress handler — each aborting mid-flight into an ordinary worker dispatch, so each is correct whether or not the pool's expectation was right. The row hint survives demoted to avoiding *wasted* aborts, which is the whole difference: if every hint were wrong the caps would abort every attempt and the library would behave as it does today, slower by the wasted decode. Two mechanics had to be discovered. `SQLITE_OMIT_PROGRESS_CALLBACK` was in the build defines, so the enforcement point exp 265 named did not exist in the shipped library; compiling it back in is below the floor (-0.31% / +0.07% / -2.19% over four order-flipped passes, the most opcode-heavy lane coming out fastest), because SQLite reaches the check only at jump-back opcodes. And the handler cannot be a Dart callback: it fires inside `sqlite3_step`, which the decoder enters as an `isLeaf` call, and a leaf call cannot re-enter Dart — the VM aborts the process — so the decision lives in C, which also resets the per-statement VM-step counter that would otherwise make a cheap statement abort spuriously every few hundred executions. The fourth failure, microtask coalescing, exp 265 called a design question with no obvious cheap answer, and a new `frame-jitter` lane (worst lateness of a 60 Hz timer during a 50 ms read burst) shows it was right to worry: with the budget unreachable, worst-case frame lateness is 33,344 us — two frame intervals to within 10 us, every deadline in the sample missed. A 1 ms per-event-loop-turn stopwatch retired by a zero-duration Timer takes it to 1147 us against dispatch's 2381 us, so the design is *better* on frame time than the pool it bypasses, for 2.8% of its throughput win. Three collections of four alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes, six independent `ab_drift_check` verdicts per lane, all reproduced: point read -60 to -62%, 21-column point read -65%, 20-row page -37 to -39%, 64-row page at the cap -22 to -25%, and a point read issued while four 1,000-row reads hold the whole pool -89% (admission cost, not transfer). `concurrent8`, written by exp 265 as the lane that could kill the idea, is -68%: parallelism cannot recover a per-request overhead larger than the request. Costs are a +29 to +37% once-per-statement abort when a hint mispredicts, +0.8-1.2 MB of peak RSS for the fifth reader connection, and a +2.8% residue on the one TEXT-heavy control — reduced from +4.5% by passing a sentinel so the shared decode loop's cap check is an unconditional compare rather than a guarded one, and at the floor of a lane that reads +34.9% between two binaries differing only by a compile flag. Thirteen routing tests assert the counters rather than the data, and were verified to fail against a build with enforcement removed, since an unbounded inline read returns entirely correct rows.
